Q: Is there any way to get key hash from signed APK? A:

On linux, I used this command to get the key hash from an apk:

keytool -list -printcert -jarfile [path_to_your_apk] | grep -Po "(?<=SHA1:) .*" |  xxd -r -p | openssl base64

For Mac Users (OS X) as there is no grep -P support

keytool -list -printcert -jarfile ~/Downloads/YOURAPKFILE.apk | grep "SHA1: " | cut -d " " -f 3 | xxd -r -p | openssl base64

Q: Is it legal for the compiler to degrade the time complexity of a program? Is this considered observable behavior? A:

The C standard doesn't actually have a time complexity model, neither for its primitive operations, nor its library functions, so compilers are allowed to do pretty much anything that preserves program semantics (observable behavior).

The C++ standard only gives complexity guarantees only for some its library functions, and says (17.5.1.4 [structure.specifications]):

Complexity requirements specified in the library clauses are upper bounds, and implementations that provide better complexity guarantees satisfy the requirements.

A compiler better preserve these bounds (and since many of the functions are templated/may be inlined, the compiler is involved), but the bounds are in terms of the number of elements in containers and restrict the number of calls to comparison operators and the like. Otherwise, the compiler is again free to do as it pleases.

Q: How to change $_ value before condition check A:

I finally figured out what the problem was. The reason turned out to be simple.

Not all Active Directory users have Exchange mailboxes, and those without mailboxes have a null-valued msExchMailboxGuid property. Passing a null ($null) value to the [guid]::new constructor causes an error Exception calling ".ctor" with "1" argument(s): "Value cannot be null. Parameter name: b . The error text itself tells us that we shouldn't pass a null value to the constructor. But who reads error messages anyway, right? ))

So the solution is to filter out AD users whose msExchMailboxGuid property value is $null.

But anyway, @mklement0, I am grateful to you for your help, your links are very useful, I learned a lot of new things of the PowerShell basics.

Q: Inner case expression is throwing an error when trying to sum the values A:

You didn't name the amount column in your t subquery.

select sum(t.amount)
from
(select yearquarter,
       (case when sum(case when type not in (3, 4) then 1 else 0 end) = 0
             then sum(amount)
             else sum(case when type not in (3, 4) then amount else 0 end)
        end) AS amount
from t
where status = 'A'
group by yearquarter)t;

Q: Convert case expression to logical operator in the where clause A:

You can translate it to boolean logic in this way:

WHERE  @reftype = '0 'OR @refnum = 'n/a' 
OR (@reftype = 'BN' AND @refnum = refbn)
OR (@reftype = 'C'  AND @refnum = refc)
OR (@reftype = 'O'  AND @refnum = refo)

But note that CASE in the WHERE-clause is not inefficient per se.

Q: Using less than symbol in CASE expression A:

You can do it even easier:

SELECT FirstName, LastName, Salary, 
CASE WHEN salary < 40000 THEN 'Low Pay'
WHEN salary < 70000 THEN 'Medium Pay'
ELSE 'High Pay' END AS PayRange
FROM Employees;

Q: Software engineering A:

In some places its also a legal thing. In Canada, to be called an engineer you legally have to pass the professional engineering exam. Which doesn't really have any use for software, so pretty much nobody does it. As a result, companies hiring in Canada call the position software developer so they don't have to legally hire someone who has. You will sometimes see companies hiring in the US or Canada and will see the job listing say the title will be "software engineer" in the US and "software developer" in Canada.
